item.description:
Snapline 2.8.1

A reliability and privacy release: every finding from a full audit of the app, fixed.

Privacy

  • Redactions are now unrecoverable by default. New redactions use a solid box — blur and pixelate remain available, with a note that blurred text can sometimes be reconstructed.
  • Redacting a screenshot while its text was still being indexed can no longer leave the pre-redaction text searchable.
  • With Smart Redact after capture, the un-redacted original is now kept privately in Snapline's own storage instead of your screenshots folder — so raw captures never sync to Desktop, Dropbox, or iCloud locations.
  • Auto-copied captures are marked as concealed, so clipboard managers no longer archive them.
  • Turning off "Index text in screenshots" right after launch now purges reliably, and the on-disk index is readable only by your account.

Never lose an edit

  • Clicking Done, Pin, or Copy with a caption still being typed now includes that text in the saved image.
  • Quitting immediately after a capture no longer loses the capture's History entry, and quitting after a recording keeps its duration badge.
  • Editing or relocating your archive is now crash-safe — a crash at the wrong moment can no longer drop entries from History.
  • A save that fails (full disk, unmounted volume) now says so instead of failing silently.

Fixes

  • Cancelling Tall Capture during startup no longer leaves the screen-recording indicator on.
  • Clicking a shape to select it no longer disturbs undo/redo.
  • The Quick Access card no longer slides away underneath an open Save dialog.
  • Changing the translation language mid-translation now reliably restarts it.
  • Combining many large captures no longer spikes memory before reporting the size limit.
  • Many smaller fixes across capture, recording, trimming, and licensing.

Choose what the text index keeps

A new privacy setting — Index text in screenshots, in Settings → History, on by default — governs what text recognition keeps, never what it can read.

  • Off purges the index: the background indexer stops, and every recognition record already stored — text, code payloads, cached translations — is deleted behind a confirmation that states exactly how many entries it covers.
  • Everything still works: Copy Text, the Text window, code detection, and translation read the capture on demand and keep nothing. History search falls back to filenames and dates, and the empty state says so.
  • Nothing is lost but the stored text: re-enable the setting and your captures are indexed again, automatically.

Updates come straight from snap-line.app

The update feed and update downloads are now served from our own domain. From this version on, the app contacts only snap-line.app — no request from the app reaches a third-party host. Nothing to do; updates keep arriving exactly as before.

Help, one keystroke away

A new Snapline Help window — from Help… in the status menu, or ⌘? in any Snapline window — so what the app can do is never more than a click from where you are.

  • Shortcuts: a cheat sheet grouped by surface — Capturing, After a capture, History, Editor — showing your actual bindings, live. Change a shortcut in Settings and the sheet follows; an unbound action stays listed, greyed, with a link straight to the Shortcuts pane.
  • Features: the capability tour — capture modes, editor tools, Smart Redact, Copy Text, QR & barcode detection, Translation, History, pinning, export — each with a one-liner, including the ones you'd otherwise only find by accident.
  • A real Help menu joins the menu bar, so ⌘? and macOS's own help search work the way they do everywhere else.

Recordings keep every second

A recording that ended on a still screen used to lose its tail: the file stopped at the last moment anything changed on screen, so ten seconds of recording could save as a five-second movie. Recordings are now anchored to the moment you press stop.

  • Still time is recorded time: the last frame holds until the moment you stopped, however long the screen sat still — and the menu-bar timer keeps counting through still stretches, always reading what the file will hold.
  • Pauses cut exactly the paused span: still time on either side of a pause stays in the recording, and a recording resumed onto a still screen starts counting again immediately. Only the time between pause and resume is removed.
  • Stopping is immediate and safe: the file is finalized before the capture stream is torn down, so a slow teardown can no longer cost recorded seconds — and the moment you press stop, the menu bar swaps the red recording control for a quiet "finalizing" glyph frozen at the recording's final length.
  • GIF export holds the last frame for its full duration, so a converted recording lasts exactly as long as the movie it came from.
